questions.q: WannaCry, the global outbreak of May 2017 that encrypted systems and demanded bitcoin payments, was:
questions.solution: WannaCry was ransomware - it encrypted victims' files and demanded ransom (in bitcoin), spreading via the EternalBlue exploit against unpatched Windows.
questions.shortcut: Encrypt + demand money = ransomware; WannaCry is the stock example.

questions.q: The Rehearse Timings feature is used to:
options: Record the time spent on each slide for automatic advance
Time the download of the file
questions.solution: Rehearse Timings records how long each slide stays on screen while you practise, then can auto-advance the show using those durations - essential for self-running kiosks.
questions.shortcut: Practise now, auto-advance later - that is Rehearse Timings.

questions.q: The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 by:
questions.solution: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the WWW at CERN in 1989 and wrote the first browser. Vint Cerf co-designed TCP/IP; Larry Page co-founded Google.
questions.shortcut: Web = Berners-Lee, 1989, CERN. Internet (1970s TCP/IP) = Cerf and Kahn.

questions.q: Assembly language mnemonics such as ADD and MOV are converted into machine code by a(n):
questions.solution: An assembler translates assembly (2GL) mnemonics into machine language. Compilers/interpreters work on high-level (3GL) languages; preprocessors transform source text before compilation.
questions.shortcut: Assembly -> Assembler (same first letters); high-level -> compiler/interpreter.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said, "Alas! I am ruined."
options: He said with sorrow that he is ruined.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he is ruined.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he was ruined.
He exclaimed with joy that he was ruined.
questions.solution: Alas → **exclaimed with sorrow**; am → was (backshift); I → he. B inverts the tone; C leaves the tense; D strands 'is'.
questions.shortcut: Alas = sorrow; am → was.

questions.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Water is the source of all life. **P:** Industries release effluents into the rivers. **Q:** Groundwater levels are falling every year. **R:** We must harvest rainwater without delay. **S:** Cities dump untreated sewage into the same rivers. **6.** Otherwise the taps of tomorrow will run dry.
questions.solution: **P** (industrial pollution) → **S** (city sewage, 'the same rivers' needs P's rivers) → **Q** (falling groundwater completes the crisis) → **R** (the remedy) before S6. PSQR.
questions.shortcut: 'The same rivers' locks S after P; remedy (must) sits last before S6.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

No sooner he **arrived** than the power supply failed.
questions.solution: *No sooner* at the start demands inversion + *than*: **did he arrive** (base form after *did*). 'Had he arrive' mixes the *had* inversion with a base form, and 'he did arrive' is not inverted.
questions.shortcut: No sooner → did + subject + base verb + than.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3).
questions.solution: 'Years later, Arun, now a software engineer, still ___ that pen' — the sentence describes Arun's present habit (note *now*, *still*), with singular subject Arun: **keeps**. *Kept* would clash with 'now/still'; *keep* lacks agreement; *keeping* is not finite.
questions.shortcut: 'Still + now' marks a living present habit → simple present with -s.

questions.q: The boundary between the Earth's crust and the mantle is called the:
questions.solution: The **Mohorovičić (Moho) discontinuity** separates the crust from the mantle. Gutenberg separates mantle and core, Lehmann separates outer and inner core, and Conrad lies within the crust.
questions.shortcut: 'Come Make Good Lunch' — Moho is second.

questions.q: The **Shaka era**, used for India's national calendar, was started in 78 CE by —
questions.solution: The Shaka Samvat (78 CE) is traditionally credited to the Kushana king **Kanishka**. It was adopted as the base of India's **National Calendar** (from 22 March 1957). Vikram Samvat starts in 57 BCE.
questions.shortcut: "57 minus, 78 plus" — 78 CE = Kanishka's accession.

questions.q: Evidence of a **ploughed field** belonging to the Harappan period has been discovered at —
questions.solution:
**Kalibangan** (Hanumangarh, Rajasthan, on the Ghaggar) shows a ploughed field with criss-cross furrows, plus fire altars. The name means 'black bangles'.

Trap: Banawali (Haryana) has a **clay model** of a plough, not a field.
questions.shortcut: **Kali**bangan = **Kheti** (field). Model plough → Banawali.

questions.q: The Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin), VB-G RAM G, which replaced MGNREGA, guarantees:
options: 100 days of employment per household, as under MGNREGA
125 days of wage employment per rural household per year, effective 1 July 2026
questions.solution: The VB-G RAM G Act (2025) raises the statutory guarantee from 100 to **125 days** per rural household per financial year and came into force on **1 July 2026**, with weekly wage payments replacing the 15-day cycle.
questions.shortcut: 125 days from 1-7-2026 — 'quarter-century more, from July'.

questions.q: If 40% of a number is 256, then 55% of that number is:
The mean of the cubes of the first 6 natural numbers is:
questions.solution: Sum of cubes $=\left[\frac{6\times7}{2}\right]^2=21^2=441$. Mean $=\frac{441}{6}=73.5$.
questions.shortcut: $\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2/n$: $441/6=73.5$. Trap: 441 (the sum, not the mean).

questions.q: 12 men can complete a piece of work in 15 days. In how many days will 20 men complete the same work?
questions.solution: $12 \times 15 = 20 \times D$ ⇒ $D = 9$ days.
questions.shortcut: 180 man-days ÷ 20 men = 9 days.

questions.q: In an isosceles triangle $ABC$, $AB=AC=25$ cm and $BC=14$ cm. The area of the triangle is:
questions.solution:
The median/altitude to the base: $h=\sqrt{25^2-7^2}=24$ cm.

Area $=\frac12\times14\times24=168\ \text{cm}^2$.
questions.shortcut: 7-24-25 again: height 24, area $=\frac12\times14\times24=168$. Trap: 336 forgot the $\frac12$.

questions.q: Select the related number: **2 : 8 :: 3 : ?**
questions.solution: 8 = 2³, so the relation is **cube**. 3³ = **27**. (×4 would give 12 and square-plus-4 gives 13 — neither is offered; the cube reading is the intended, and only surviving, rule.)
questions.shortcut: When b = a² or a³ exactly, the answer is the same power of the probe — 8 and 27 scream cubes.

questions.q: Chef : Kitchen — choose the pair with the **same** relation:
questions.solution: Relation: professional to the **place of work**. Judge works in a court ✓. Tailor : Fabric is worker-material, Teacher : Student is worker-person served, Doctor : Medicine is worker-object used.
questions.shortcut: Same-relation selection: test every option against one sentence — 'second is where the first works'.
questions.pattern: select the pair with the same relation

questions.q: Introducing a boy, a girl said, **"He is the son of my father's only son."** How is the boy related to the girl?
questions.solution: My father's only son = the girl's brother (the girl is a daughter, so 'only son' is her brother). The boy is her brother's son → her **nephew**.
questions.shortcut: 'Only son' of her father cannot be the girl — she is female — so it is her brother.

questions.q: Select the related word: **Zoology : Animals :: Entomology : ?**
questions.solution: Relation: branch of study to its **subject**. Entomology is the study of **insects**. (Ornithology → birds, Ichthyology → fishes, Pedology → soil.)
questions.shortcut: Study bank: entomology-insects, ornithology-birds, ichthyology-fishes, etymology-word origins.
questions.pattern: word analogy from the standard relation bank
